Corporate reputation management is the ongoing process of monitoring, protecting, and improving how people perceive your company. It covers what customers, employees, investors, and job seekers believe about you, and why.

The key word is ongoing. Reputation isn’t something you fix once and then put on the back burner. It’s shaped by every post, policy, and customer interaction (online and off), so managing it means paying attention all the time.
Tracking what people say about your company across social, news, and review sites
Responding to complaints and concerns with tact

It’s also a team sport. Marketing, social, customer support, and leadership all influence your company’s reputation, whether they think of it that way or not.

Why does corporate reputation management matter?
Corporate reputation management matters because reputation affects almost every number your company cares about, including sales, hiring, retention, and even market value.

A strong reputation gives people a reason to choose your company. A damaged one can make them think twice, whether they’re considering buying your product, applying for a job, or investing in your business.
Here’s how it affects different audiences:
People buy from companies they trust, full stop. 88% of consumers say trusting a brand is a deal breaker when making a purchase, according to a 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer study.

They also do their homework. A customer might check Google reviews and scroll your comments. A B2B buyer might read G2 reviews or ask peers in a Slack community. Either way, they’re sizing up your reputation before they take the next step.
Your employees live with your company’s reputation every single day. A good reputation gives them something to be proud of. A bad one makes them update their LinkedIn between meetings.

Employees are also your most believable brand champions, and the data backs it up: 74% of U.S. adults say employees do more to shape a company’s brand than traditional marketing, according to a 2026 Harris Poll study.
That’s what makes employee advocacy so powerful.

Investors watch reputation closely because it signals risk. A company with a history of leadership controversies, lawsuits, or angry customers looks like a riskier bet, even if the numbers look fine today.
A steady brand reputation gives investors confidence that the business can weather a rough quarter (or a rough headline).

83% of job seekers are likely to research company reviews and ratings before they apply, according to Glassdoor. If what they find is negative, your best candidates may never hit “apply.” That makes hiring slower, more expensive, or both.

Corporate reputation is driven by the quality of your product, how you treat customers and employees, how your leaders behave, and what others say about you online. Your messaging plays a role, but it can’t cover for a bad product or an unpleasant support team.

Product or service quality: This is the foundation. If your product breaks, ships late, or falls short of its promises, no amount of clever marketing can fix it. The reverse is also true: a product or service people really love does a lot of reputation work for you.

Customer experience: People remember how you made them feel, especially when something went wrong. A fast, friendly fix can turn a frustrated customer into a loyal one. Social media has also raised the stakes: 62% of consumers now expect a response within an hour when reaching out through social media or online forums.
Leadership: What your executives say and do reflects on the whole company. That includes interviews, LinkedIn posts, earnings calls, and how they respond when things go sideways.
Company culture: Your company culture isn’t as private as you think. It shows up in Glassdoor reviews, Reddit threads, and the occasional viral TikTok from an unhappy employee.
Transparency: Nobody expects a company to be perfect. But people do expect honesty. How you handle legitimate concerns makes a big difference to your reputation.

AI answers: Tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude pull information about your company from news coverage, online reviews, and even social media posts. If those sources are mostly negative or outdated, they can send the wrong impression.
Some of these factors are well within your control. Others aren’t. The good news is, you can still take steps to influence your brand image.
How do you manage corporate reputation?
You can manage corporate reputation by understanding where you stand today, monitoring what people say, and building a clear plan for who responds and how.
Here’s the process, step by step:
Set up monitoring across social, news, and reviews
Define sentiment and volume thresholds for alerts
Reinforce positive voices and employee advocacy
Before you can improve your reputation, you need an honest picture of it. Start by gathering what’s already out there, including:
Recent news coverage and social conversations about your company
Review ratings on sites like Google, G2, Trustpilot, and Glassdoor
How AI tools describe you (for example, open an AI chatbot and ask “What is [company] known for?”)
Feedback from sales calls, support tickets, and employee surveys
Psst: Don’t just look for complaints. Note what people consistently praise, too. That can tell you what’s already working, so you know what to amplify.
2. Set up monitoring across social, news, and reviews
Once you know where you stand, the next step is keeping tabs on current conversations. The easiest way to do this is with a social listening tool.
Company and product names (including common misspellings)
Competitors, so you can see how you compare
A tool like Lumen tracks all of the above, plus reviews, surveys, and customer feedback from up to 300 sources.
3. Define sentiment and volume thresholds for alerts
Not every negative comment is a crisis. One angry tweet is normal. Two hundred angry tweets within an hour is a different story.
Thresholds help your team tell the difference. Decide in advance what level of activity should trigger an alert, and how urgent that alert should be.
Brand mentions spike 2-3x above normal, or negative sentiment rises noticeably
Brand mentions spike 5x+ above normal, a negative story gets media coverage, or a serious safety or legal concern emerges
Keep in mind: Some issues deserve immediate attention, even if only one person is talking about them. A credible safety complaint, for example, shouldn’t have to go viral before someone investigates.
Reputation management involves several teams. Without clear ownership, you risk having five people respond to the same issue. Or worse, nobody responds at all.
Rick Pendrick, Founder and CEO of Prism PR, has seen how costly that confusion can be.

“At NASCAR, I handled executive and crisis communications for our Chairman and CEO, and the crises that went worst were never the ones with the worst facts. They were the ones where people spent the first morning arguing about who was in charge.”

The fix is to settle those questions before a crisis hits. Pendrick recommends a decision tree that spells out “who makes the call, who speaks, and who signs off.” That way, your first hour goes toward strategizing, not debating.
Speed matters, but not at the expense of clarity. A reply on X that contradicts your statement on LinkedIn creates a second problem on top of the first.
Prevent any messaging mixups by preparing pre-approved response templates for common situations, like service outages or shipping delays. These give your team a strong head start.
6. Reinforce positive voices and employee advocacy
Reputation management is more than just putting out fires. It’s also about elevating positive stories.

A glowing review could become a social post. A customer who keeps singing your praises might be a great fit for a case study. Flag these moments as they come in, so they don’t get buried under everything else.
Then, bring your employees into the mix. Give them an easy way to share company news and wins. That’s where an employee advocacy platform comes in handy.
Set aside time each month to check how your reputation is trending.
When something changes, dig into why. Maybe a pricing update sparked a wave of complaints, or changes to your onboarding process led to fewer complaints.
Then, share what you find with the teams that can act on it. Fixing the issue at its source will do more for your reputation than responding to the same complaint over and over.

How do you handle a reputation crisis?

You handle a reputation crisis by first assessing the situation and deciding whether a public response is needed. If it is, acknowledge the issue quickly, keep your messaging consistent, and follow through until the problem is resolved.
Here’s what that looks like in practice:
Not every negative story needs a public statement. Sometimes responding to a minor criticism draws more attention to it. Other times, staying silent puts speculation into overdrive.
So before you respond, consider how serious the issue is, who’s affected, and whether people need information from your company.
For example, if your entire website goes down, your customers need to know you’re aware of it. On the other hand, some issues are better handled one-on-one.
“If the issue truly touches only a few people and fixing it privately makes them whole, handle it directly with them,” says Pendrick.
That cheerful promo post you scheduled last week? It can read very differently in the middle of a crisis. Put your content calendar on hold until you’ve checked that nothing upcoming will land badly.
Psst: If you’re using a scheduler like Perch, you can pause all scheduled content in just a few clicks.
Choose one place for official updates, like a status page or pinned post, and point every channel back to it. That keeps your message consistent and gives people one place to check for updates.
If the situation is ongoing, don’t disappear after your first statement.
Share your progress regularly, even when the update is “still working on it.” Then, once things are fixed, explain what you’re changing so it doesn’t happen again.
Own your mistakes and follow through
If your company messed up, say so. Explain what went wrong, take responsibility for your part, and tell people what you’re doing to make things right.
Then actually do it. A good apology can help repair trust, but real recovery comes from fixing the problem that caused the crisis in the first place.

Take CrowdStrike, for example. In the summer of 2024, the cybersecurity company pushed a faulty software update that crashed millions of Windows computers worldwide. It quickly became known as one of the biggest IT outages in history. Not a great look for a company whose whole job is keeping systems safe.

Its CEO apologized publicly the same day, and the company later published a detailed breakdown of what went wrong. A few weeks after that, CrowdStrike’s president showed up in person to accept a tongue-in-cheek “Most Epic Fail” award at a major hacker conference.
The humility quickly paid off. By early 2025, CrowdStrike recovered about $30 billion in market value.
How do you measure corporate reputation?

You measure corporate reputation by tracking how people feel about your company and how those perceptions change over time. There’s no single metric that tells the whole story, so you’ll want to look at a mix of social, customer, employee, and media data.
Here are the metrics to track:
Brand sentiment: The share of positive, neutral, and negative mentions about your brand. A sudden dip can be an early warning sign of a crisis.
Share of voice: How much of the conversation in your industry is about your brand versus competitors. Most social listening tools will track this for you.
Trust scores: How much customers, employees, or the public trust your company, usually measured through surveys. Net Promoter Score (NPS) and employee engagement surveys are common starting points.
Online reviews: Your average rating on sites like Google, G2, Trustpilot, and more.
Media coverage: How much press you’re getting, where it’s coming from, and whether the tone is positive or negative.
One tip: Make sure to set a baseline before you need it. A 10% drop in sentiment only means something if you know what “normal” looks like.

Some of the biggest mistakes in corporate reputation management come down to poor communication. Getting defensive, hiding criticism, sending conflicting messages, or making promises you can’t keep can all chip away at people’s trust.
Here are the most common mistakes to avoid:

Arguing with critics in public. Even when you’re technically right, a back-and-forth in your comment section almost never makes a brand look good. Whenever possible, take heated conversations to DMs or email.
Deleting negative comments. Trying to hide criticism is a common gut reaction. But unless a comment breaks your community guidelines, deleting it can look like you have something to hide.
Sending conflicting messages. If your social team says one thing but your CEO says another, people won’t know what to believe. Make sure everyone is working from the same information.
Over-promising. Making big promises in the heat of the moment is tempting, but only commit to what you can realistically deliver.
Ultimately, reputation management takes a cool head. Thoughtful, honest responses will do more for your reputation than halfhearted attempts at damage control.

Corporate reputation management is the ongoing process of monitoring, protecting, and improving how people perceive your company. It covers everything from your public image and online presence to how customers, employees, and investors feel about your business. Good brand reputation management helps you build trust, earn customer loyalty, and reduce reputational risk over time.
What’s the difference between reputation management and PR?

Reputation management looks at the bigger picture: how people perceive your company and what you can do to influence that perception. PR is one part of that work, focused on building relationships and earning positive attention. For example, your PR team might use press releases and media outreach to share company news. Meanwhile, your broader corporate communications strategy also considers customer feedback and employee experiences.
What strategies can improve a company’s corporate reputation?

Start with the basics: deliver a quality product, treat customers and employees well, and make sure your actions reflect your brand values. From there, keep an eye on what people are saying about your company, address recurring complaints, and stay consistent in how you communicate. Over time, a strong brand presence can become a real competitive advantage.
How do online reviews affect corporate reputation?

Online reviews shape how people see your company, even before they’ve interacted with you directly. A steady stream of positive customer reviews can build trust, while negative feedback can make potential buyers think twice. That’s why review management matters. Keep an eye on your ratings, look for recurring complaints, and make responding to reviews part of your routine.
How long does it take to recover from a reputation crisis?

There’s no set timeline. Some companies recover from a minor controversy in a few weeks, while serious reputational damage can take months or years to repair. Your crisis response makes a difference, but so does the original issue. Effective crisis management means acknowledging what went wrong, keeping people informed, and following through on meaningful changes.
